nameStory: Tree swallows get their name from their habit of nesting in tree cavities, particularly old woodpecker holes in dead or dying trees near water. Unlike barn swallows that build mud nests under eaves, these aerial acrobats are cavity nesters who have adapted well to using nest boxes too. The scientific name 'bicolor' perfectly describes their striking two-toned appearance.
description: Tree swallows are sleek, streamlined birds about the size of a sparrow, built for life on the wing. Adults sport a stunning metallic blue-green back that shimmers in sunlight, contrasting sharply with bright white underparts. These agile fliers spend most of their time swooping and diving through the air, catching insects with their wide-opening beaks. You'll rarely see them perched for long, as they're constantly in motion during daylight hours.

idTips.label: Two-toned coloring
idTips.description: Adults show a dramatic split between iridescent blue-green upperparts and pure white underparts, creating a clean line along the sides that's visible even at a distance

idTips.label: Metallic sheen
idTips.description: The back and head shimmer with an oily, rainbow-like quality in good light, shifting from deep blue to green as the bird moves

idTips.label: Streamlined silhouette
idTips.description: Long, pointed wings and a slightly forked tail create a sleek torpedo shape perfect for swift, graceful flight maneuvers

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Quick, darting movements with frequent direction changes as they chase flying insects, often skimming just above water surfaces

idTips.label: Female and juvenile differences
idTips.description: Young birds and first-year females appear much duller, with brown backs instead of the metallic sheen, and may have grayish wash on the breast

habitat: Tree swallows favor open areas near water where flying insects are abundant, including marshes, ponds, lakes, and rivers throughout New England. They nest in cavities in dead trees (snags) or nest boxes placed in fields, particularly areas that were once wetlands or remain seasonally flooded. You'll often spot them hunting over mowed fields, golf courses, and agricultural areas adjacent to water sources.

seasonality.spring: Adults arrive in early May with males showing their brightest breeding plumage - that spectacular metallic blue-green sheen is at its most vivid. They're busy investigating nest sites and can be seen entering and exiting tree cavities or nest boxes.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity as they're constantly hunting insects to feed their young, making them highly visible as they dart over fields and water. Young birds fledge in midsummer, appearing much browner and duller than their parents.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks gather in preparation for migration, sometimes creating spectacular aerial displays over marshes and fields. The metallic sheen may appear slightly less vibrant as feathers begin to wear.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England as they migrate to southern coasts and Central America, though climate change is causing some to linger later into fall than in previous decades.

funFact: Tree swallows are one of the few songbirds that can survive on berries alone when insects become scarce, allowing them to migrate later than other swallows and sometimes even survive brief cold snaps by switching to a vegetarian diet of bayberries and other fruits.
confusionNotes: Young tree swallows with their brown backs can be confused with bank swallows, but tree swallows are larger and lack the distinct brown breast band that bank swallows wear like a necklace. Adult tree swallows are easily distinguished from the rusty-red barn swallow by their clean white (not peachy) underparts.
contextualKnowledge: Tree swallows have become a model species for scientific research, with thousands of studies conducted on their behavior, genetics, and ecology. This means we know more about tree swallow biology than almost any other songbird, making them excellent ambassadors for understanding bird life cycles and conservation needs.
compareHints: As the only Tachycineta swallow regularly found in New England, tree swallows are most easily compared to other local swallows. They're larger and more robust than bank swallows, which have brown backs and distinct breast bands. Unlike barn swallows with their deeply forked tails and rusty underparts, tree swallows have only slightly forked tails and pure white bellies.
